name: Verizon Business
category: Global carrier managed SD-WAN / SASE provider
evidence_summary: Verizon source evidences managed SASE/SD-WAN leader positioning; Versa partner source evidences managed platform with SD-WAN, security, routing, multi-tenancy and analytics.
cost_model: Quote-based managed service; typically platform, access, security bundle, sites/users/bandwidth/term.
key_differentiators: Global carrier-led managed SASE and SD-WAN with strong North American presence and international delivery.
Versa Networks partnership provides multi-tenant SD-WAN platform with security, routing and analytics under managed service.
Established reputation as a SASE managed services leader in industry analyst rankings.
best_fit_for: North American and multinational enterprises wanting carrier-led managed SD-WAN and SASE.
Buyers comfortable with Versa as the underlying platform via managed delivery.
Organisations prioritising service maturity and global delivery capability.
watch_outs: Platform is largely Versa-based; buyers wanting platform optionality should evaluate alternatives.
Commercial model is bespoke; cost transparency and change governance require careful contracting.
DIY/self-managed model is not the primary positioning.
verification_notes: Re-verified 2026-07-29 against named primary sources. Every graded fact carries a source, a tier and a verbatim quote confirmed present on the cited page by an independent check. Industry, region, organisation-size and pricing evidence was sourced on the same basis. Facts that could not be sourced are published as unknown with the reason. The value_tier field is a Netify assessment of relative cost position, not a supplier claim: most of this market publishes no price. Sources found and rejected are listed at tier 4.

ai_capability.note: Network Detection and Response analytics; platform AI depends on the chosen vendor.

resilience.note: Private IP global MPLS plus managed dual-vendor designs.

profile.platform_architecture: Verizon Business runs one of the largest managed WAN practices globally, built on its Private IP MPLS heritage and a multi-vendor SD-WAN portfolio spanning Cisco (Catalyst and Meraki), VeloCloud, Versa and Fortinet. Global delivery is mature: 150+ countries through owned assets and partners, with professional services to match complex, multi-region migrations.
profile.security_sase: Managed SASE combines the SD-WAN portfolio with leading SSE platforms (Zscaler, Palo Alto and others) plus Verizon's own security services including Network Detection and Response and the long-running DBIR threat research. Security operations capability is genuine carrier-grade; platform depth follows the chosen vendor stack.
profile.service_support_channel: Fully managed and co-managed with 24x7 follow-the-sun operations and named service management. US heritage with substantial UK and European delivery. Verizon suits complex global RFPs where contractual accountability across dozens of countries is the requirement.
profile.commercials_verdict: Per-site managed pricing on multi-year terms, quote based and negotiable at scale. The Netify verdict: shortlist Verizon for large multinational estates, especially with Americas weight, MPLS migrations at scale and security-conscious boards: the multi-vendor bench means the platform fits the estate rather than the reverse. UK-only mid-market buyers will find nimbler fits elsewhere.

vendor_faqs.q: Which SD-WAN vendors can Verizon manage?
vendor_faqs.a: Cisco Catalyst and Meraki, VeloCloud, Versa and Fortinet feature in Verizon's portfolio, with SSE pairings including Zscaler and Palo Alto. Verizon proposes against your estate; you are buying their delivery and operations as much as the platform.

vendor_faqs.q: How strong is Verizon outside the Americas?
vendor_faqs.a: Genuinely global: 150+ country delivery through owned network and partners, with established UK and European operations. Americas-weighted multinationals get the most value from the asset base.

vendor_faqs.q: Does Verizon help with MPLS to SD-WAN migration?
vendor_faqs.a: Yes, it is core business: Verizon runs large Private IP estates and migrates them to hybrid and internet-first SD-WAN designs with professional services, co-existence patterns and global circuit management.

shortlist_summary: Verizon bring carrier-scale managed SASE and SD-WAN with a strong North American presence and international delivery capability that extends well beyond the US. Typically shortlisted alongside AT&T for large enterprise and multinational deployments, the choice between the two often coming down to existing carrier relationships and where the majority of sites are located.
cost_note: Carrier-scale managed pricing on multi-year terms; premium incumbent positioning.
uk_basis: UK contracting entity (Verizon Business has UK operations), though US headquartered, with real UK and European delivery.

f01_fully_managed_service.quote: From fully managed to monitor/notify only, Managed SD Branch offers flexible management options that give you the control you need
f01_fully_managed_service.note: Verizon states a fully managed option explicitly and in its own words. The Managed SD WAN page reinforces it ('Get peace of mind by allowing our experts to plan, monitor, manage and secure your network'), and the NaaS SLA makes the managed scope contractual by applying only to 'Verizon managed NaaS components'. End-to-end design, deploy, monitor, change, support and report is the standing Verizon operating model across the reviewed pages.

f03_co_managed_service.quote: From fully managed to monitor/notify only, Managed SD Branch offers flexible management options that give you the control you need
f03_co_managed_service.note: Graded partial deliberately. This sentence evidences a spectrum of management options between fully managed and monitor/notify only, which implies shared responsibility, but no page reviewed sets out a named co-managed tier with a defined split of policy authorship and change rights between Verizon and the customer. The definition requires the customer to retain selected policy and change rights, and that specific division was not found verbatim in sources 3, 4, 8, 9 or 6.

f04_multi_tenant_msp_white_label_support.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. The Verizon Partner Solutions wholesale SD-WAN page (source 18) does market Managed SD-WAN to Service Providers, stating 'Verizon Managed SD-WAN has the ability to enable Service Providers to quickly realize this opportunity', but it is silent on every element the definition actually requires: tenant isolation, delegated administration, branded customer portals and reusable templates enabling an MSP to operate the platform under its own brand. Selling wholesale to service providers is not the same as white-label multi-tenancy, so an inference either way would be unsafe. Also checked sources 3, 4, 9 and the Verizon Enterprise Center portal references without result.

f05_professional_services_and_migration_.quote: Verizon brings decades of expertise in designing, transitioning, implementing and managing SD WAN networks.
f05_professional_services_and_migration_.note: Design, transition and implementation are claimed directly, corroborated by the SASE landing page ('We have 20 years of experience in the design, deployment, and management of network and security infrastructure') and by the existence of a contractual Professional Services Service Attachment in the service guide (source 17). Confidence held at medium because the granular elements named in the definition, specifically discovery workshops, pilots, staging, migration runbooks, rollback plans and training, were not found verbatim on any page reviewed; the 2020 professional services index lists no network migration SOW by name.

f07_lifecycle_management.quote: Verizon Care is an equipment maintenance service that provides advanced parts replacement with on-site repair support.
f07_lifecycle_management.note: Graded partial for two reasons. First, scope: hardware replacement and on-site repair are documented, and the CPE page adds procurement, deployment, maintenance and refresh, but firmware upgrades, patching, licence renewals and end-of-life planning were not found verbatim. Second, and more important for the definition, Verizon Care is presented as a separately purchasable equipment maintenance service rather than something inherently bundled into the Managed SD-WAN or SASE service, so the 'as part of the service' test is only partly met on the evidence reviewed.

f17_cellular_and_5g_support.quote: Whether you have Verizon wireline or wireless access, SD Branch can support both.
f17_cellular_and_5g_support.note: Graded partial rather than yes. Wireless access as a supported transport is stated plainly, and the same page describes a wireless backup option, which covers the failover half of the definition. However the words '5G', '4G' and 'LTE' do not appear in this context, and SIM management and signal monitoring were not found on any page reviewed (sources 3, 4, 8, 9, 21). Verizon is of course a mobile network operator, but that is prior knowledge and cannot be graded from; only what the pages state is reflected here.

f19_public_cloud_gateways.quote: Integrates network operation centers (NOCs) and security operation centers (SOCs) with our Managed SD WAN and Virtual Network Services (VNS), and supports Versa, Cisco cEdge and vEdge, Zscaler ZIA, Zscaler ZPA and Palo Alto Prisma Access.
f19_public_cloud_gateways.note: This is the pivotal judgement in the record. The cloud gateways that actually enforce security and deliver remote access in Verizon's SASE service are Zscaler Internet Access, Zscaler Private Access and Palo Alto Prisma Access, all of which run on those vendors' own global PoP estates, not Verizon's. Verizon's service guide carries a Zscaler product description (source 12) confirming it resells those subscriptions. Verizon operates substantial infrastructure of its own, but that is the MPLS and IP transport layer, not a Verizon-built cloud security edge, so the definition forces partner_integrated rather than yes. An identical vendor list was found on both the UK and US product pages, so this is not a regional arrangement.

f20_private_pops_dedicated_pops.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. No page describes customer-hosted, dedicated or sovereign PoP deployments as an alternative to shared multi-tenant locations. Specifically checked the UK and US SASE product pages (sources 8, 9), the Private IP page (source 10) and the SD Branch page (source 4), and ran a targeted search for Verizon sovereign or dedicated SASE PoPs which returned only generic private-IP-addressing explainer pages. Note that on-premises security enforcement is offered ('SD Branch manages SD WAN (and other) services and can optionally employ either premises-based or cloud-based security mechanisms'), but premises-based security appliances are not the same thing as a dedicated PoP, so this is recorded as unknown rather than inferred.

f21_private_global_backbone.quote: Private IP is a MultiProtocol Label Switching (MPLS) network that connects locations and clouds around the globe in 185+ countries.
f21_private_global_backbone.note: Comfortably meets the definition and is not a single-country case. Verizon operates a genuinely global MPLS backbone reaching 185+ countries, the Private IP page states 'Traffic is completely separated from the public internet to help keep it secure', and source 11 carries the ownership claim 'we own and operate one of the largest and most reliable networks on the planet'. Inter-region predictability is contractually underwritten by the Private IP SLA (source 7), which commits to jitter of '< 5 ms' PE to PE for EF class and a packet delivery ratio of '99.995%' for EF, exactly the sort of between-PoP commitment the definition contemplates.

f26_sla_backed_service_fabric.quote: This SLA only applies to Verizon managed NaaS components on a NaaS Order.
f26_sla_backed_service_fabric.note: Among the strongest evidence in this record because it rests on contractual documents rather than marketing pages. Three separate published SLAs were read. The NaaS SLA (source 6) commits to tiered site availability, to repair response of '3.5 hours (US)' or '4 hours (rest of world)' for managed devices, and to proactive incident notification 'within 15 minutes of opening such Priority 1 Trouble Ticket'. The Private IP SLA adds latency, jitter and packet delivery ratio standards. This is contractual rather than best-effort, covering uptime, response and incident handling together.

f27_integrated_next_generation_firewall.note: The full NGFW feature set is present in the delivered service: the Versa partner page lists IDS/IPS alongside 'Antispam, antimalware and URL filtering' and DLP, and the SASE pages describe firewall as a service. But every one of those functions is another company's technology that Verizon bundles and manages, named on Verizon's own pages as Versa, Cisco cEdge and vEdge, Palo Alto Prisma Access and Zscaler, with the SASE landing page adding Netskope and Viptela. No evidence was found of a Verizon-authored firewall engine. Under the definition's explicit instruction, third-party firewall technology that the supplier resells or bundles grades partner_integrated, not yes.

f33_data_loss_prevention.note: DLP is available in the service, evidenced from two independent Verizon-hosted Tier 1 documents: the Versa partner page lists it as a delivered capability, and Verizon's own Zscaler product description names 'core data protection capabilities (such as data loss prevention essentials and out-of-band CASB essentials)'. In both cases the inspection and classification engine belongs to the partner (Versa, Zscaler), so partner_integrated. Caveat recorded honestly: the alerting and exception workflow element of the definition was not found verbatim on either page, so the grade rests on the classify-and-block half of the definition.

f40_managed_service_assurance.quote: Support provided by Verizon's Network Operations Center (NOC) and Security Operations Center (SOC) teams
f40_managed_service_assurance.note: Both a NOC and a SOC are Verizon's own and wrap the partner technology, which is the core of the definition. Proactive ownership is contractual rather than merely claimed: the NaaS SLA commits Verizon to open a trouble ticket for each Priority 1 incident and notify the customer within 15 minutes. The SOC services page adds 'Gain 24/7 access to monitoring, extensive global threat visibility and expert analysis', and SD Branch confirms '24/7/365 access to Managed SD Branch reporting'. Confidence is medium rather than high because two named elements of the definition, formal root cause analysis and structured periodic service reviews with change governance, were not found verbatim on any page reviewed.

delivery_model.quote: We partner with leading SASE vendors including Palo Alto, Zscaler, Versa Networks, Viptela and Netskope.
delivery_model.note: Verizon Business does not author the SD-WAN or SSE software it sells. Every SASE and SD-WAN page reviewed describes Verizon operating and managing other vendors' technology (Versa, Cisco cEdge/vEdge, Zscaler ZIA/ZPA, Palo Alto Prisma Access, Netskope, Viptela) across its own network and its own NOCs and SOCs. Verizon does author the surrounding operational layer (NaaS Management Center, Verizon Enterprise Center portal) and owns the underlying carrier network, but no evidence was found that it authors a SASE product, so 'managed_provider' rather than 'both'.

underlay_ownership.quote: We have more than 160,000 employees around the world, and we own and operate one of the largest and most reliable networks on the planet.
underlay_ownership.note: Verizon states network ownership directly, and unlike most SASE suppliers on this shortlist it is a facilities-based carrier: it runs its own Private IP MPLS core and publishes contractual PE-to-PE latency, jitter and packet delivery standards for it (source 7), which a pure reseller could not underwrite. Confidence is held at medium rather than high for one specific reason: the Private IP footprint spans 185+ countries, which in practice must involve third-party local access outside Verizon's owned footprint, but no page reviewed documents those off-net arrangements. If that off-net detail were published the honest value might be 'mixed'. Graded from what the pages state, not from what the footprint implies. Caveat on the source: page 11 cites a 2016 investment figure and is partly stale, so it was used only for the ownership sentence.

sse_layer_ownership.quote: We partner with leading SASE vendors including Palo Alto, Zscaler, Versa Networks, Viptela and Netskope.
sse_layer_ownership.note: Palo Alto Networks (Prisma Access), Zscaler (ZIA and ZPA), Versa Networks, Netskope, and Cisco (cEdge and vEdge, plus Viptela). Verizon did not build its security service edge; it integrates, sells and operates other vendors' stacks. This is stated by Verizon itself on the exact landing page under assessment and independently confirmed on both the UK and US SASE product pages, which give the same vendor list. Verizon's service guide even hosts a Zscaler product description document (source 12), which is about as direct as resale evidence gets. Directly analogous to the BT and Fortinet example. Verizon's own build is the wrapper (NaaS Management Center, NOC and SOC integration, Verizon Enterprise Center), not the enforcement stack.

regulatory_documentation.quote: Learn how to get to the root of your payment security strategy to better address PCI DSS v4.0 compliance requirements.
regulatory_documentation.note: Frameworks found named on Verizon pages: PCI DSS v4.0 and the SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework (CSCF). Frameworks specifically searched for and NOT found as attestations: ISO 27001, SOC 2, NIS2, DORA, NHS DSPT, GDPR and HIPAA. The distinction that decides this grade is that every framework named appears in a customer-advisory context, Verizon selling assessment and consultancy to help customers reach compliance, not as an attestation covering Verizon's own SASE or SD-WAN service. An ISO 27001 statement of work exists in the service guide but it is a Professional Services SOW that Verizon performs for customers, again not a Verizon certification. No trust centre or certification schedule for the SASE service was located, so this is 'not_found' rather than 'assurance_only'; there is not even a general sentence claiming the SASE platform meets regulatory standards.

pop_count.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. The only PoP figures located anywhere on verizon.com are in source 19, which on inspection is the 1998 MCI WorldCom merger announcement, not a current Verizon Business document: it reads 'MCI WorldCom will bring together the Internet expertise of UUNET and MCI to create one of the world's largest providers of Internet services with over 2,000 points-of-presence around the globe' and, contradicting itself elsewhere on the same page, 'over 1,000 Points of Presence (POPs) throughout the United States and in Canada, Europe and the Asia-Pacific region'. Those describe a predecessor company nearly three decades ago and are internally inconsistent, so neither can be reported as Verizon Business's current PoP count. The networks overview page and Private IP page publish reach figures instead of PoP counts (185+ countries and territories; services in more than 150 countries). Separately, because the SASE security PoPs are Zscaler's and Palo Alto's estates rather than Verizon's, any Verizon PoP figure would not be the relevant number for a SASE comparison in any case.

sla_availability_pct.quote: Verizon will maintain the Availability for each Site Type as detailed below, with MLAN and MWLAN Network Components meeting the Functionality Threshold, if applicable.
sla_availability_pct.note: Read this figure with care. Verizon does not publish one headline availability number; it publishes a tiered table keyed to site type, quoted from the NaaS SLA as 'Highly Available Large Medium Small Extra Small 100% 99.95% 99.90% 99.50% 99.00%'. The 100% figure applies only to a 'Highly Available' site, meaning a dual-CPE resilient design. The realistic figures for standard sites are 99.95% (Large), 99.90% (Medium), 99.50% (Small) and 99.00% (Extra Small). Two other SLAs read in this task give different numbers again for different services: the Global Private IP SLA commits to 99.9% end-to-end for Gold, 99.5% for Silver and 97.0% for Bronze, and the Adaptive Network Fabric SLA states 'The Service is designed to maintain 99.9% Port Network Availability per billing cycle'. These are different products rather than contradictions, but a like-for-like comparison against a single-number SASE vendor should probably use 99.95% rather than 100%. Recorded in conflicts.

sectors.healthcare.quote: Deploying a Verizon SASE solution helped a large healthcare business optimize its security operations.
sectors.healthcare.note: Two separate supplier sources tie SASE specifically to healthcare. The SASE product page carries the short proof point quoted here, and a longer written case study describes a diversified healthcare company where Verizon Network-as-a-Service provided the foundation with SASE layered on, covering users across all 200 sites. The customer is not named in either. Healthcare also has a dedicated industry page in Verizon's industry index.

sectors.financial_services.quote: A slow and dated network kept this retail bank from moving its business into the future.
sectors.financial_services.note: Two distinct SD-WAN banking case studies exist. The retail bank story is quoted here. A second story on a leading bank states it Deployed SD WAN architecture and private IP circuits with 4G LTE backup. Both customers are anonymised, which is why this is vendor-claimed rather than independently verifiable, but the sector and the SD-WAN solution are explicit in both. Financial services also has a dedicated industry page.

sectors.retail_ecommerce.quote: Deploy network monitoring and cloud security services to address core network security, and leverage mobile solutions to help ensure data security across all your devices.
sectors.retail_ecommerce.note: Graded yes on the dedicated retail industry page plus a retail digital connectivity sub-page whose SD-WAN section carries retail-specific network visibility copy, and an SD-WAN article that treats retail as one of three named use cases. Confidence is medium rather than high because there is no named retail customer and no retail SD-WAN or SASE case study anywhere in the material read. Buyers should not read this as equivalent to the healthcare, financial services or manufacturing evidence.

sectors.manufacturing.quote: Verizon Professional Services provided a detailed plan for SD WAN design and roll-out, while engineers prepared the manufacturer's LANs.
sectors.manufacturing.note: The strongest sector in this set. There is both an SD-WAN case study, quoted here, describing a global build book, LAN refresh and MPLS offload, and a separate SASE case study describing a UK-based manufacturing business reducing physical firewalls through zero trust network access. Both customers are anonymised. Manufacturing also has a dedicated industry page.

sectors.energy_utilities.quote: Dakota Valley Electric Cooperative powers efficiency with Verizon Grid Wide.
sectors.energy_utilities.note: Verizon has a dedicated energy and utilities industry page carrying the one named utility customer quoted here. Graded partial rather than yes because that named proof is a Grid Wide smart-grid deployment, and the page contains no SD-WAN or SASE narrative content at all beyond global navigation menu links. Sector presence is real, SASE and SD-WAN proof for the sector is absent.

sectors.government_public_sector.quote: Network modernization, full lifecycle communications integration, mobility, secure collaboration, managed security services.
sectors.government_public_sector.note: Graded yes on two dedicated public sector routes. The federal EIS contract vehicle page, quoted here, lists network virtualisation SD-WAN as in-scope modernisation and links managed network services. The state and local government solutions page separately lists Managed SD WAN with US-based support and Secure Access Service Edge among its products. A US federal contract vehicle is a published framework for the sector, which meets the yes bar directly. Evidence is US-specific; no equivalent UK or European public sector framework was found in the pages read.

sectors.education.quote: A Managed SD WAN solution can provide intelligent control over network services to improve performance for students and faculty without expensive infrastructure upgrades.
sectors.education.note: The clearest sector-plus-product statement found anywhere in this research. Verizon's dedicated education page names Managed SD WAN and states the education-specific benefit in a full sentence. No named education SD-WAN customer, but the dedicated industry page with product-specific copy meets the yes bar on its own.

sectors.transport_logistics.quote: Connecting workers to high-speed networks can help unlock the full potential of automation, robotics and other technologies needed to drive warehouse transformations.
sectors.transport_logistics.note: Verizon has a dedicated distribution and logistics industry page carrying several genuinely named customers including GSM Outdoors, Nucor, Penske and Associated British Ports. Graded partial rather than yes because every one of those named engagements is private 5G, IoT or warehouse connectivity, and neither SD-WAN nor SASE appears in the page content. This is the case where the temptation to over-grade is strongest, since the named-customer density is high, but none of it is SASE or SD-WAN evidence.

sectors.professional_services.quote: the industries with the highest percentage of remote and hybrid working arrangements are information, financial activities, and professional and business services
sectors.professional_services.note: The sector is named only inside a general SD-WAN thought-leadership article, as market commentary about hybrid working rather than as a Verizon capability claim. There is no dedicated professional services industry page in Verizon's industry index and no customer or case study. This is a list mention and nothing more, which is exactly the partial definition.

sectors.hospitality_leisure.note: No sector-specific evidence found. Checked: the industry solutions index, which lists Live entertainment but has no hospitality or leisure entry and whose live entertainment page returned HTTP 404; the en-gb Travel and Hospitality resource hub, which rendered as navigation and a subscription form with no network, SD-WAN or SASE content; and the full customer success stories index, where the closest entries are sports venue, stadium and bar fixed wireless stories that are 5G and fixed wireless access rather than SD-WAN or SASE. Recording unknown rather than inferring from the venue connectivity work.

regions.uk_ireland.note: Best-evidenced region outside the US. A SASE case study explicitly identifies the customer as a UK-based manufacturing business migrating off Verizon's global MPLS network, which is delivery evidence rather than a sales presence claim. Verizon also publishes separate per-country contractual terms for both the United Kingdom and Ireland under its EMEA terms index, and runs a dedicated en-gb site.

regions.europe.note: Verizon publishes per-country contractual terms pages for a long list of European countries including Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Ukraine and the United Kingdom. Per-country terms indicate a contracting entity and service relationship, which is materially stronger than the locale switcher on the product pages.

regions.north_america.note: Home market. Beyond the global statistic quoted here, Verizon holds US federal contract vehicles including EIS and GSA MAS that explicitly carry SD-WAN and managed network services, and the state and local government page advertises Managed SD WAN with US-based support. Canada appears as its own contracting region in the terms index. Direct delivery, not partner-mediated.

regions.asia_pacific.note: Verizon's terms index publishes Asia Pacific as a contracting region with per-country terms pages for Japan, Australia, Hong Kong, China, India, South Korea, Malaysia, New Zealand, Pakistan, Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan and Thailand. Confidence is medium rather than high because no APAC points of presence, SD-WAN availability statement or APAC customer case study was found in the pages read, so this rests on contractual footprint rather than published service coverage.

regions.middle_east_africa.note: Graded partial deliberately. Although Verizon brands the region EMEA, the actual per-country terms list contains only Morocco, South Africa and Turkey outside Europe. No Gulf states, no wider African coverage, no MEA points of presence and no MEA customer evidence were found. The regional brand name substantially overstates the evidenced footprint, so partial is the honest grade.

regions.latin_america.note: Verizon publishes Latin America as a distinct contracting region with per-country terms pages for Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Panama, Peru and Venezuela. Confidence is medium because this is contractual footprint evidence only. No Latin American points of presence, SD-WAN availability statement or customer case study was found.

regions.china_mainland.note: China appears by name in Verizon's own Asia Pacific per-country terms list, which is more than a generic global claim and is why this is partial rather than unknown. However the China terms page itself returned HTTP 404, so the licensing arrangement, the local entity and the actual services deliverable in mainland China could not be verified. No SD-WAN or SASE availability statement for mainland China was found. Treat any Verizon global coverage figure as saying nothing about China and require the arrangement to be confirmed directly with the supplier.

organisation_fit.large_global_enterprise.quote: Learn how Verizon helps power enterprise and medium businesses with a broad portfolio of secure technology solutions that are built to power scale and growth.
organisation_fit.large_global_enterprise.note: Explicit targeting plus matching case study size. Verizon's own segmentation defines Enterprise as 500+ employees, and the published SD-WAN and SASE case studies are all large multi-site organisations: a global manufacturer rolling out a build book around the world, a bank with thousands of locations, a healthcare company across 200 sites and a UK manufacturer operating in over 200 countries. This is clearly the primary target.

organisation_fit.mid_market.quote: Learn how Verizon helps power enterprise and medium businesses with a broad portfolio of secure technology solutions that are built to power scale and growth.
organisation_fit.mid_market.note: Explicitly named in the supplier's own segment positioning, which is why this is yes. Confidence is medium because Verizon's published size bands are only Small and medium-sized business 1 to 499 employees and Enterprise 500+ employees, so there is no distinct mid-market product tier, no mid-market pricing and no mid-market SD-WAN or SASE case study. The targeting claim is real but the supporting proof is thin.

organisation_fit.small_business.quote: Available to businesses with 19 employees or less.
organisation_fit.small_business.note: Verizon runs a substantial small business division, but the small business security product is Business Internet Secure, capped at the headcount quoted here, and it is a broadband and device security bundle rather than SASE or SD-WAN. No small business SD-WAN or SASE tier, packaging or price point was found in any page read. Graded partial to reflect that Verizon serves the segment but not with this product line.

published_pricing.note: No price is published that we could quote. The value_tier field on this record is a Netify assessment of relative cost position, not a supplier claim.
